result.question: If hydrogen starts climbing on Transformer 1 at site MAIN, I want my operators to know what to suspect and what to check next. Using our known transformer failure modes, list every mode where rising hydrogen is a meaningful signal. For each one, say which one or two companion channels would confirm it, choosing from methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, co, co2, oxygen, dbds, dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v and oti. Then look at the actual data between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 and tell me which of those modes the companion channels currently support. Run a DGA fault classification on the latest complete sample as a tie-breaker. Keep the list to the modes where hydrogen genuinely helps tell them apart, not every mode. If hydrogen didn't rise across the window, say so, but still give the watch-list, and label every mode as 'not currently indicated' rather than ranking them.
result.answer:
Nothing further to fetch — I have the failure-mode list, the 4-sample window, and the DGA tool returned "LLM unavailable" on two attempts, so I computed the IEC 60599 ratios manually for the tie-breaker.

## Hydrogen trend, Transformer 1 (MAIN), 2024-01-15 → 2024-01-18

| Date | H2 | CH4 | C2H6 | C2H4 | C2H2 | CO | CO2 | O2 | DBDS | Diel. | IFT | OTI |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 01-15 | 2845 | 7406 | 5467 | 16684 | 7 | 32 | 1344 | 5860 | 19 | 55 | 45 | 85 |
| 01-16 | 2950 | 7200 | 5400 | 16500 | 6 | 30 | 1300 | 5700 | 18 | 53 | 44 | 87 |
| 01-17 | 2800 | 7300 | 5500 | 16700 | 8 | 35 | 1350 | 5900 | 20 | 56 | 46 | 84 |
| 01-18 | 2900 | 7350 | 5450 | 16600 | 7 | 33 | 1325 | 5800 | 19 | 54 | 45 | 86 |

**Hydrogen did not rise across the window.** It oscillated 2800–2950 ppm (net +55 ppm, +1.9%, non-monotonic, within sample-to-sample noise). Absolute level is very high (~2,900 ppm) but it is a stable plateau, not a climb. Every companion channel is likewise flat. Per your instruction, all watch-list modes below are labelled **not currently indicated** and are not ranked.

## Hydrogen watch-list (modes where a rising H2 actually discriminates)

| Failure mode | Why H2 matters | Confirming companion(s) | Status (this window) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Partial Discharge in Oil | H2 is the dominant/near-only gas | **methane** (CH4/H2 < 0.1) + **acetylene** (≈0) | Not currently indicated — CH4/H2 = 2.5, far from PD signature |
| Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking) | H2 rises together with a small acetylene step | **acetylene** (0.1 < C2H2/C2H4 < 1) + **ethylene** | Not currently indicated — C2H2 flat at 6–8 ppm, C2H2/C2H4 ≈ 0.0004 |
| High-Energy Arcing | H2 and acetylene surge together | **acetylene** (C2H2/C2H4 > 1) + **ethylene** | Not currently indicated — no acetylene rise |
| Thermal Fault — Oil Overheating (300–700 °C) | H2 rises as a secondary gas under a CH4/C2H6/C2H4 hydrocarbon lead | **ethylene** + **ethane** (1 < C2H4/C2H6 < 4), **oti** as corroboration | Not currently indicated as a *change* — but companion levels already sit in this band (see tie-breaker) |
| Thermal Fault — Core/Winding (>700 °C) | H2 rises alongside dominant ethylene | **ethylene** (C2H4/C2H6 > 4) + **methane** (CH4/H2 > 1), **oti** | Not currently indicated — C2H4/C2H6 = 3.05, just under the >4 threshold |

Excluded from the H2 watch-list because hydrogen doesn't help separate them: Cellulose Insulation Ageing (co/co2), Oil Dielectric Degradation (dbds, interfacial_v, dielectric_rigidity), Oil Contamination / Moisture Ingress (oxygen, dielectric_rigidity), Tap Changer Mechanical Wear (no main-tank gas signature).

## DGA tie-breaker — latest complete sample (2024-01-18)

The `interpret_dga` service was unavailable (two attempts), so IEC 60599 ratios were computed manually:

- C2H2/C2H4 = 7 / 16600 = **0.0004** → code 0
- CH4/H2 = 7350 / 2900 = **2.53** → code 2
- C2H4/C2H6 = 16600 / 5450 = **3.05** → code 2 (borderline with T3 at >4)

Classification: **T2 thermal fault, 300–700 °C** (hydrocarbon-dominated, no acetylene, ethylene leading), i.e. the standing gas mix is consistent with **Thermal Fault — Oil Overheating**, bordering on Core/Winding hot-spot. OTI at 84–87 °C is consistent with a thermally-stressed unit. This is a baseline condition of the oil, not a new development in the window; it explains *why* H2 is at 2,900 ppm, but does not constitute the rising-H2 trigger you asked about.

## What operators should check if H2 does start climbing

1. Re-sample and confirm the rise is > ~10% over consecutive samples (current noise band is ±3%).
2. Check **acetylene** first — any rise above the 6–8 ppm floor moves the suspicion from thermal to arcing (High-Energy if C2H2/C2H4 > 1).
3. If acetylene stays flat, check **methane** — CH4/H2 dropping below 0.1 points to Partial Discharge; staying >1 keeps it thermal.
4. If thermal, watch **ethylene vs ethane** — C2H4/C2H6 crossing 4 shifts the call from oil overheating to core/winding hot-spot; corroborate with **oti** rising above the current 84–87 °C.
